lessons.title: Your C Code Becomes a Real Binary -- No Class Needed
lessons.description:
Your first C program isn't run by an interpreter -- gcc compiles it straight into a native binary your OS executes directly. In under a minute, see how hello.c turns into ./hello, why return 0 matters, and why C skips the class wrapper you'd expect coming from Java.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/c-mastery-path/level-1/01-setup/

#Shorts

questions.question: In `gcc hello.c -o hello`, what does the -o flag do?
questions.explanation: The -o flag tells the compiler what to name the output binary, so here it produces a file named "hello".
printf writes the text to standard output and \n is a newline escape sequence, not a literal backslash-n.

questions.question: Why does hello.c start with `#include <stdio.h>`?
options: It links the program to the operating system kernel
It defines the main function's entry point
It is required to declare integer variables
It pulls in declarations for standard I/O functions like printf before compilation
questions.explanation: The #include directive is a preprocessor step that pulls in declarations for functions like printf before compilation proper begins.

lessons.title: C's Sneaky Integer Overflow Bug (No Warning!)
lessons.description:
Add 1 to the largest int C can hold, and something strange happens: no crash, no warning, just a silent flip to the most negative number possible. This is integer overflow, and it's one of the first surprises new C programmers hit once they understand fixed-size types. We walk through INT_MAX and why C won't stop you from wrapping around.

Source lesson:
https://sigilipelli.github.io/c-mastery-path/level-1/02-variables-data-types/

#Shorts

questions.question: Why is reading an uninitialized variable in C considered undefined behavior?
options: C requires every variable to be declared inside a function
C does not zero out variables for you, so an uninitialized one holds garbage until assigned
The compiler refuses to compile programs with uninitialized variables
questions.explanation: The compiler doesn't automatically zero out variables, so an uninitialized one holds whatever garbage was already in that memory.

options: A compile error, since dividing ints requires an explicit cast
4, because C rounds to the nearest integer
3, because integer division discards the fractional part
3.5, because C always performs real division
questions.explanation: Since both operands are int, this is integer division and the fractional part is discarded, not rounded, giving 3.

questions.question: Which operator lets you ask the compiler for a type's size, like `sizeof(int)`?
questions.explanation: sizeof lets you ask the compiler for a type's size at compile time instead of assuming a fixed width.

lessons.title: C's switch Fallthrough: The Bug With No Warning
lessons.description:
In C, forgetting a break inside a switch statement doesn't trigger a compiler error -- it just silently changes what your program does. This Short breaks down switch fallthrough: why it happens, how it trips up nearly every C beginner at least once, and when experienced C devs actually use it on purpose.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/c-mastery-path/level-1/03-control-flow/

#Shorts

questions.question: What happens if you forget a `break` statement inside a switch case?
options: The switch statement is skipped entirely
Execution falls through into the next case
questions.explanation: Omitting break causes execution to fall through into the next case instead of exiting the switch, which trips up most C beginners at least once.

options: It prints 10 once, since do-while checks the condition after the body runs
It loops forever printing increasing numbers
It prints nothing, since 10 < 5 is false
questions.explanation: A do-while loop always runs its body at least once before checking the condition, so it prints 10 even though 10 < 5 is false.

questions.question: Which keyword skips the rest of the current loop iteration and jumps to the next one?
questions.explanation: continue skips the remaining code in the current iteration and moves on to the next one, unlike break which exits the loop entirely.

lessons.title: Why Your C Function Can't Change the Original Variable
lessons.description:
C passes every argument by value — your function gets a copy, not the real thing. In this Short we break down a classic C gotcha: why incrementing a parameter inside a function leaves the caller's variable completely untouched, and what actually fixes it.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/c-mastery-path/level-1/04-functions/

#Shorts

questions.question: Why does a function often need a prototype declared before it's called earlier in the file, like before main?
options: Without a prototype, the linker deletes the function
C requires functions to be declared in alphabetical order
The compiler reads top to bottom and needs the function's signature to check a call before seeing its definition
Prototypes make the program run faster at runtime
questions.explanation: The compiler reads a file top to bottom, so a prototype lets it verify a call's correctness before it has seen the actual function definition.

options: Outside: 5, because C passes arguments by value so increment only modifies its own local copy
A compile error, because n is reused as a parameter name
Outside: 5, due to a compiler bug
Outside: 6, because increment permanently changes x
questions.explanation: C copies each argument's value into the function's parameter, so changes inside increment never affect the caller's original variable x.

questions.question: Which keyword makes a local variable keep its value between function calls instead of resetting each time?
questions.explanation: Marking a local variable static makes it persist between calls while still staying scoped to its own function.

lessons.title: The One-Symbol Fix for C's Pass-by-Value Problem
lessons.description:
In C, functions get a copy of whatever you pass them -- so why does swap() actually work? The answer is pointers: pass an address, dereference it, and you're touching the caller's real memory. This is the core idea behind pointers in C, straight from the C Mastery Path curriculum.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/c-mastery-path/level-1/06-pointers-basics/

#Shorts

questions.question: Why is it good practice to initialize a pointer to NULL and check it before dereferencing?
options: The compiler requires all pointers to start at NULL
NULL pointers make code run faster
Dereferencing an uninitialized pointer holding a garbage address is undefined behavior and a common cause of crashes
Assigning NULL automatically frees the pointer's memory
questions.explanation: An uninitialized pointer holds a garbage address, and dereferencing it is undefined behavior that commonly crashes programs.

options: x=10, y=10, because both parameters point to the same variable
x=5, y=10, because C is always pass-by-value and swap can't change x and y
x=10, y=5, because passing addresses lets swap modify the caller's actual variables
A compile error, since swap expects int arguments, not pointers
questions.explanation: By passing &x and &y, swap receives the addresses of x and y and can dereference them to modify the caller's actual variables.

questions.question: Which operator both declares a variable as a pointer and means "dereference" in an expression?
questions.explanation: The * symbol marks a pointer declaration like `int *p`, and in an expression like `*p` it means dereference the address p holds.

lessons.title: C Fundamentals, Start to Finish: Variables, Control Flow, Functions, Pointers & Structs (Level 1)
lessons.description:
This is a complete walkthrough of Level 1 of the C Mastery Path, stitched into one continuous lesson. We start with how C stores values in memory -- variables, types, casting, and the integer overflow bug that catches everyone eventually -- then move through control flow (including the switch-fallthrough trap), functions and recursion, pointers (the concept that makes C feel different from everything else), and finally structs, the building block for every custom data type you'll write. Each section builds on the one before it, so watch in order if you're new to C.

Lessons covered in this video:
- Variables, Data Types & Operators: https://sigilipelli.github.io/c-mastery-path/level-1/02-variables-data-types/
- Control Flow: https://sigilipelli.github.io/c-mastery-path/level-1/03-control-flow/
- Functions: https://sigilipelli.github.io/c-mastery-path/level-1/04-functions/
- Pointers Basics: https://sigilipelli.github.io/c-mastery-path/level-1/06-pointers-basics/
- Structs: https://sigilipelli.github.io/c-mastery-path/level-1/07-structs/

Source lesson(s):
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/c-mastery-path/level-1/02-variables-data-types/
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/c-mastery-path/level-1/03-control-flow/
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/c-mastery-path/level-1/04-functions/
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/c-mastery-path/level-1/06-pointers-basics/
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/c-mastery-path/level-1/07-structs/

questions.question: What is the purpose of writing `typedef struct {...} Point;` instead of just `struct Point {...};`?
options: typedef allocates memory for the struct's members
typedef is required only for structs with nested structs inside them
Struct definitions are invalid without typedef
typedef creates an alias so you can write just the type name instead of repeating "struct" every time
questions.explanation: typedef creates a type alias, so code can write Point instead of struct Point everywhere it's used.

options: A compile error, since pointer arithmetic isn't allowed on arrays
10, because *(numbers + 1) is the same as numbers[0]
20, because numbers[i] and *(numbers + i) are equivalent ways to access the same element
questions.explanation: An array name decays to a pointer to its first element, so *(numbers + 1) is equivalent to numbers[1], which is 20.

questions.question: In a recursive factorial function, what stops the recursive calls from continuing forever?
options: The semicolon at the end of the function body
The compiler automatically halts after 10 recursive calls
The base case, where n <= 1 returns 1 instead of making another recursive call
questions.explanation: The base case (n <= 1 returning 1) stops the recursion; without a reachable base case the calls would continue until a stack overflow.

lessons.title: Go Programs Run Without Go Installed -- Here's How
lessons.description:
Most languages need their runtime installed everywhere your code runs -- Go doesn't. One `go build` gives you a single static binary you can copy to any machine with the same OS and architecture, and it just runs. This is lesson 1 of the Go Mastery Path: installing Go, writing your first program, and understanding go run vs go build.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/go-mastery-path/level-1/01-setup/

#Shorts

questions.question: Why does every runnable Go program need a func main() inside package main?
options: It's the entry point the Go runtime looks for
It registers the file with gofmt
questions.explanation: Go programs execute starting from func main() in package main, which produces an executable.

questions.question: Given `go run main.go` prints "Hello, world!", what did that command actually do?
options: Compiled to a temporary binary, ran it, then cleaned up
Formatted the file and exited without running it
Only checked the syntax without executing anything
Compiled to a permanent binary and left it on disk
questions.explanation: go run is for quick iteration: it builds a temporary binary, executes it, and removes it afterward.

questions.question: Which command rewrites a Go file in place using Go's standard formatting style?
questions.explanation: gofmt -w rewrites the given file in place so it matches Go's one true formatting style.

lessons.title: Go Refuses to Add an Int and a Float (On Purpose)
lessons.description:
Coming from Python or JavaScript? Go will stop you cold the moment you try to add an int and a float64 without converting first. This isn't a bug — it's Go's way of making every type conversion, and every bit of lost precision, explicit and visible right in your code.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/go-mastery-path/level-1/02-variables-types-operators/

#Shorts

questions.question: Why must you write float64(i) + f instead of i + f when i is an int and f is a float64?
options: Go never converts types implicitly, so mixing them is a compile error
The + operator only works on strings by default
float64 values cannot be added to anything
Go automatically rounds ints to match floats
questions.explanation: Go requires explicit conversion between numeric types; mismatched types in an expression fail to compile.

questions.question: Given `const ( StatusPending = iota; StatusActive; StatusDone )`, what value does StatusActive hold?
questions.explanation: iota starts at 0 and increases by one per line, so the second constant, StatusActive, becomes 1.

questions.question: Which declaration keyword is required for a variable declared at package level?
questions.explanation: The short declaration := only works inside function bodies, so package-level variables must use var.

lessons.title: Go's switch Breaks a Classic C Habit -- On Purpose
lessons.description:
In C or Java, forgetting a break in a switch statement is a classic, silent bug. Go flips the default: every case breaks automatically, and you have to opt in with the fallthrough keyword if you actually want execution to spill into the next case. One keyword swap removes a whole class of switch-statement bugs.

Source lesson(s):
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/go-mastery-path/level-1/03-control-flow/

#Shorts

questions.question: Why does Go get by with only one looping keyword, for?
options: for is required only for range expressions
while loops are handled by a separate keyword
for covers every case other languages split across for/while/do-while
Go doesn't allow loops without labels
questions.explanation: Go unifies classic, while-style, and infinite loops under the single for keyword.

questions.question:
With day := "Tue", what does this switch print?
switch day {
case "Sat", "Sun":
  fmt.Println("Weekend")
case "Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri":
  fmt.Println("Weekday")
default:
  fmt.Println("Unknown")
}
questions.explanation: "Tue" matches the second case listing weekdays, so "Weekday" is printed.

questions.question: Which keyword must you add to a switch case to make it fall into the next case?
questions.explanation: Go switch cases don't fall through automatically; fallthrough opts into that behavior explicitly.

lessons.title: Go Doesn't Have Exceptions -- It Has This Instead
lessons.description:
Go's signature move: a function can hand back two values at once, usually a result and an error, right there in the return type. Watch divide() handle a division-by-zero without a single try/catch, and see why Go won't let you quietly ignore an error you declared.

Source lesson(s):
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/go-mastery-path/level-1/04-functions-multiple-returns/

#Shorts

questions.question: Why is the blank identifier _ needed when calling divide(10, 0) and ignoring the numeric result?
options: Go forces you to either use every declared variable or explicitly discard it
error values must always be paired with _
Go requires _ for all float64 return values
questions.explanation: Go won't let a declared variable go unused, so _ explicitly discards the value you don't need.

questions.question:
What order do these lines print in?
fmt.Println("start")
defer fmt.Println("cleanup (runs last)")
fmt.Println("middle")
questions.explanation: defer schedules the call to run right before the function returns, so it prints after "middle".

questions.question: In what order do multiple defer statements in the same function execute?
questions.explanation: Deferred calls stack up and run in LIFO order when the surrounding function returns.

lessons.title: This Go Slice Trick Will Silently Corrupt Your Data
lessons.description:
Slicing a slice in Go doesn't copy anything -- it hands you a window into the exact same memory. Change one, and you might silently change the other too. Here's the gotcha, and the one function that actually fixes it.

Source lesson(s):
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/go-mastery-path/level-1/05-arrays-slices-maps/

#Shorts

questions.question: Why does modifying view[0] after view := original[1:4] also change original?
options: Slices are always sorted before use
Slicing doesn't copy data, so both slices share the same backing array
Go copies slices by value automatically
questions.explanation: A slice is a view over an underlying array, so two slices from the same source can share memory.

questions.question: If ages has no "Eve" key, what does `value, ok := ages["Eve"]; fmt.Println(value, ok)` print?
questions.explanation: A missing key returns the zero value silently, and ok is false to signal the key wasn't present.

questions.question: What idiom distinguishes a map key that's absent from one present with a zero value?
options: The nil check on the map itself
The comma-ok idiom: value, ok := m[key]
questions.explanation: The second return value, ok, is the only reliable signal that a key actually exists in the map.

lessons.title: Go Fundamentals in 9 Minutes: Variables to Pointers
lessons.description:
Go is built around one guiding idea: fewer ways to do things, and a compiler that never lets ambiguity slide. This walkthrough moves through six core lessons from Level 1 of the Go Mastery Path, in the order they build on each other -- how Go stores and converts data, how it makes decisions with if and switch and its single for keyword, how functions return multiple values and capture state in closures, how slices and maps actually share memory under the hood, how structs group data as value types, and finally how pointers let you reach back into the caller's original data. Each section pulls real, runnable code straight from the lessons so you can follow along and try it yourself in a local .go file.

Lessons covered in this video:
- Variables, Types & Operators: https://sigilipelli.github.io/go-mastery-path/level-1/02-variables-types-operators/
- Control Flow: https://sigilipelli.github.io/go-mastery-path/level-1/03-control-flow/
- Functions & Multiple Returns: https://sigilipelli.github.io/go-mastery-path/level-1/04-functions-multiple-returns/
- Arrays, Slices & Maps: https://sigilipelli.github.io/go-mastery-path/level-1/05-arrays-slices-maps/
- Structs: https://sigilipelli.github.io/go-mastery-path/level-1/06-structs/
- Pointers: https://sigilipelli.github.io/go-mastery-path/level-1/07-pointers/

Source lesson(s):
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/go-mastery-path/level-1/02-variables-types-operators/
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/go-mastery-path/level-1/03-control-flow/
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/go-mastery-path/level-1/04-functions-multiple-returns/
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/go-mastery-path/level-1/05-arrays-slices-maps/
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/go-mastery-path/level-1/06-structs/
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/go-mastery-path/level-1/07-pointers/

questions.question: Why does original stay {1 2} after calling tryToModify(original) on a Point struct?
options: Assigning or passing a struct copies it, so the function modifies a copy
Structs are always passed by reference in Go
Struct fields are immutable once set
The function must return a value for changes to persist
questions.explanation: Go structs are value types, so passing one to a function copies it and leaves the caller's original untouched.

questions.question:
What does this print?
x := 42
p := &x
*p = 100
fmt.Println(x)
questions.explanation: Writing through the pointer with *p = 100 changes the value x actually points to, so x becomes 100.

questions.question: What does iota do inside a const (...) block?
options: Generates a random constant value each run
Resets to 0 at each const block and increments by one per line
Must be manually incremented on every line
Only works when constants are strings
questions.explanation: iota is the standard idiom for auto-numbering a set of related constants starting from zero.

lessons.title: Java Doesn't Actually Need javac (Since Java 11)
lessons.description:
You've probably heard Java always makes you compile before you can run anything. Since Java 11, that's no longer true -- you can run a .java file directly, no javac step required. This short walks through the classic Hello, world program and shows both ways to run it.

Source lesson(s):
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/java-mastery-path/level-1/01-setup/

#Shorts

questions.question: Why is Java's main method declared static?
options: So it can be overloaded with different parameter lists
So it can return a value to the caller
So it can directly access private instance fields
So the JVM can call it without creating an instance of the class first
questions.explanation: static means the method belongs to the class itself, so the JVM can invoke main without instantiating an object.

questions.question: Given `public class Hello { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("Hello, world!"); } }`, what does running `java Hello` after compiling print?
questions.explanation: System.out.println prints the given text followed by a newline to standard output.

questions.question: Which command compiles a Hello.java source file into JVM bytecode?
questions.explanation: javac compiles .java source into .class bytecode files, while java runs the already-compiled bytecode.

lessons.title: Why 10 / 3 Isn't 3.33 in Java
lessons.description:
Java's integer division doesn't round -- it silently truncates. If you're dividing two ints and expecting a decimal back, you're in for a surprise the first time it bites you in production math. Here's the one-line cast that fixes it, straight from the Java Mastery Path curriculum.

Source lesson(s):
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/java-mastery-path/level-1/02-variables-data-types/

#Shorts

questions.question: What does declaring a variable as `final`, like `final double PI_APPROX = 3.14159;`, mean?
options: It can only be used inside loops
It becomes a static member of the class
It cannot be reassigned after initialization
It is automatically boxed into a wrapper class
questions.explanation: final marks a variable as unmodifiable once it has been assigned a value.

questions.question: Given `int a = 10, b = 3; System.out.println(a / b);`, what does this print?
questions.explanation: Dividing two ints performs integer division, which truncates the fractional part instead of rounding.

questions.question: What is it called when you convert a larger type to a smaller one (e.g., double to int) and must do so explicitly because data can be lost?
questions.explanation: Narrowing conversions go from a bigger type to a smaller one and require an explicit cast since precision or range can be lost.

lessons.title: Java's Switch Statement Has a Hidden Trap (Here's the Fix)
lessons.description:
Classic Java switch statements fall through to the next case if you forget a `break` -- a bug that's bitten almost every Java developer at least once. This Short shows the old fall-through-prone syntax next to the modern arrow-based switch expression (Java 14+) that removes the footgun entirely and returns a value directly.

Source lesson(s):
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/java-mastery-path/level-1/03-control-flow/

#Shorts

questions.question: Why does a do-while loop always execute its body at least once?
options: Because the body executes during compilation
Because do-while loops ignore their condition entirely
Because the condition is checked after the body runs
Because Java requires every loop to run at least once
questions.explanation: do-while runs the body first and only checks the condition afterward, so the body always executes at least once.

questions.question: Given `for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) { if (i == 5) { break; } if (i % 2 == 0) { continue; } System.out.println(i); }`, what numbers does this print?
questions.explanation: continue skips even numbers, and break exits the loop entirely once i reaches 5, leaving only 1 and 3 printed.

questions.question: In a classic Java switch statement, which keyword prevents execution from falling through into the next case?
questions.explanation: Classic switch falls through to the next case unless a break statement stops it.

lessons.title: One Method Name, Three Different Behaviors in Java
lessons.description:
Ever wonder how Java lets you call multiply(2, 3) and multiply(2.5, 4.0) and run completely different code each time? It's called method overloading, and Java picks the right version at compile time just by looking at the parameter types and count. This is one of the core ideas from Level 1 of the Java Mastery Path -- methods and parameters.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/java-mastery-path/level-1/04-methods-parameters/

#Shorts

questions.question: What allows multiply(int,int), multiply(double,double), and multiply(int,int,int) to all share the same method name in one class?
options: Java allows any methods to freely share a name
Method overloading, since their parameter lists differ
Static binding, since all the methods are static
Method overriding, since they're in different classes
questions.explanation: Overloading lets multiple methods share a name as long as their parameter lists differ in count or type, resolved at compile time.

questions.question: Given the overloaded methods `multiply(int,int)`, `multiply(double,double)`, and `multiply(int,int,int)`, what does `System.out.println(multiply(2, 3));` print?
options: A compile error due to ambiguous overloads
questions.explanation: Two int arguments match the int,int overload, which returns 2 * 3 = 6.

questions.question: Which kind of method can be called directly as ClassName.method() without first creating an object?
questions.explanation: A static method belongs to the class itself and doesn't require an instance to be called.

lessons.title: Java's ArrayList.remove() Has a Sneaky Trap
lessons.description:
ArrayList.remove() hides a classic Java gotcha: pass it an Object and it removes by value, pass it an int and it removes by index -- same method name, totally different behavior. This overload mix-up trips up beginners constantly and silently deletes the wrong element. Full breakdown of arrays vs. ArrayLists in the Java Mastery Path Level 1 lesson.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/java-mastery-path/level-1/05-arrays-collections/

#Shorts

questions.question: Why would you use an ArrayList instead of an array when you don't know how many elements you'll need in advance?
options: Because ArrayList elements are always faster to access by index
Because arrays cannot be looped over with a for-each loop
Because arrays cannot store numeric values
Because arrays have a fixed size once created, while ArrayList grows and shrinks dynamically
questions.explanation: Arrays are fixed-size once created, but ArrayList can grow or shrink as elements are added or removed.

questions.question: Given `int[] numbers = {10, 20, 30, 40}; System.out.println(numbers.length);`, what does this print?
options: A compile error because length needs parentheses
questions.explanation: length is a field on arrays (not a method call), and this array holds 4 elements.

questions.question: When you call `scores.add(95)` on a `List<Integer>`, what happens to the primitive int 95?
options: It is auto-boxed into an Integer object
It is truncated to a byte
It is stored as a primitive directly in the list
It is converted to a String
questions.explanation: Collections like List only hold objects, so a primitive int is automatically auto-boxed into its Integer wrapper.

lessons.title: Why == Says Two Equal Strings Aren't Equal in Java
lessons.description:
Two Java strings with the exact same letters, and `==` insists they're not equal. This isn't a bug -- it's `==` comparing object references instead of text, and it's one of the first gotchas every new Java developer hits. See the fix (and when `.equalsIgnoreCase` saves you a step) in the full lesson.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/java-mastery-path/level-1/06-strings-formatting/

#Shorts

lessons.title: Java Won't Let You Break Your Own Bank Account
lessons.description:
One keyword in Java stops any outside code from directly corrupting an object's data -- even your own bank account balance. This Short walks through a real BankAccount class to show how marking a field private, plus validating input in the constructor and methods, makes bad state literally impossible to write.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/java-mastery-path/level-1/07-classes-objects/

#Shorts

lessons.title: The Java Line That Runs Even After a Crash
lessons.description:
Your Java code throws an exception mid-calculation -- so what actually happens next? We walk through a real divide-by-zero crash and the one block guaranteed to run no matter what: finally. It's the key to safe cleanup code in any Java program.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/java-mastery-path/level-1/08-exception-handling/

#Shorts

lessons.title: Why 'javac' Alone Doesn't Scale (Maven Fixes This)
lessons.description:
You can compile Java by hand with javac and run it with a classpath -- it works, until your project grows past one class. This Short shows the exact commands that replace manual compiling, the standard folder layout every Maven project follows, and why that structure matters.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/java-mastery-path/level-1/09-packages-build-tools/

#Shorts

lessons.title: This Java Program Remembers Your Data After It Closes
lessons.description:
A CLI contact book built from three small Java classes -- and the trick that lets it remember every contact after the program exits. See how a Contact turns itself into a line of text to save, and rebuilds itself from that same line on load.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/java-mastery-path/level-1/10-project-contact-book/

#Shorts

lessons.title: Java Fundamentals in 10 Minutes: Variables to Classes (Level 1 Crash Course)
lessons.description:
A guided walk through the five core building blocks of Java, in the order they naturally build on each other. We start with variables, primitive types, and operators, move into control flow with if/else, switch, and loops, then package logic into methods, scale up to arrays and ArrayList, and finish by putting it all together with classes and objects. Each section pulls real, runnable code straight from the Java Mastery Path Level 1 curriculum, so you can pause and try it yourself as you go.

Because Node and browsers share the same file system

lessons.title: The JavaScript Bug That Can Never Be Fixed
lessons.description:
typeof null returns "object" -- and it's not a typo, it's a bug from JavaScript's first release in 1995 that's now permanently baked into the language for backwards compatibility. We also break down why 5 == "5" is true but 5 === "5" is false, and why you should always reach for strict equality. Pulled straight from Level 1 of the JavaScript Mastery Path.

questions.question: Why should you prefer `===` over `==` when comparing values in JavaScript?
options: Because `===` is required when comparing strings
Because `==` performs type coercion, which is a frequent source of bugs
questions.explanation: Loose equality (`==`) coerces types before comparing, while `===` checks type too, avoiding surprising results.

questions.question: Given `const nothing = null; console.log(typeof nothing);`, what gets printed?
questions.explanation: `typeof null` returns "object" — a well-known long-standing quirk of JavaScript.

questions.question: Which keyword declares a block-scoped variable that cannot be reassigned?
questions.explanation: `const` creates a block-scoped binding, and reassigning it throws a TypeError.

lessons.title: The switch fall-through trick every JS dev should know
lessons.description:
Ever seen two case labels stacked with no break between them in a JavaScript switch statement? That's not a mistake -- it's fall-through, and it's how you group multiple values under one result. This Short walks through the describeDay() example from our Control Flow lesson to show exactly how it works.

questions.question: Why does the do...while loop in the lesson log "runs at least once" even though its condition (n < 0) is false?
options: Because do...while always executes its body once before checking the condition
Because n is reset to 0 automatically
Because the condition is secretly evaluated as true
Because while loops never check their condition
questions.explanation: Unlike a plain while loop, do...while runs the body first and checks the condition afterward.

questions.question: Given the `describeDay` switch statement where "Sat" and "Sun" share a case, what does `describeDay("Sat")` return?
questions.explanation: "Sat" falls through to the same case as "Sun", which returns "weekend".

questions.question: Which keyword immediately exits a loop, as used to stop at the first multiple of 7?
questions.explanation: `break` stops the loop entirely once the condition is met.

lessons.title: Why This JavaScript Function Runs Before It's Declared
lessons.description:
JavaScript hoists function declarations completely -- but `var`, `let`, and `const` all behave differently when you reference them early. This quick breakdown shows why one gives you `undefined`, another throws a ReferenceError, and the third just works. Straight from Level 1 of the JavaScript Mastery Path.

questions.question: Why does `console.log(hoisted())` work even though it's called before the function appears in the file?
options: Because var variables keep their assigned value when hoisted
Because hoisted() is defined as an arrow function
Because function declarations are hoisted with their entire body
Because JavaScript files execute from bottom to top
questions.explanation: Function declarations are fully hoisted, so they can be called before their line in the source.

questions.question: Given nested functions each declaring their own `let x`, what does `inner()` log when called from within `outer()`?
questions.explanation: `inner()` has its own `x` set to "local", which shadows the enclosing and global variables.

questions.question: What syntax gathers extra function arguments into a real array, as in `function total(...numbers)`?
questions.explanation: Rest parameters use `...` in the parameter list to collect remaining arguments into an array.

lessons.title: JS Optional Chaining: Stop Crashing on Undefined
lessons.description:
Nested objects with a missing piece are a classic source of JavaScript crashes. Because JavaScript arrays are immutable by default
Because they throw an error if the array is changed
Because they only work on copies made with the spread operator

questions.question: Given `const nested = { profile: { social: null } }; console.log(nested.profile?.social?.twitter);`, what is logged?
questions.explanation: Optional chaining short-circuits to undefined instead of throwing when a nested property doesn't exist.

lessons.description:

questions.question: Why can `multiprocessing` achieve true parallel speedup for CPU-bound code while `threading` cannot?
options: multiprocessing disables the GIL for the current thread
Threads cannot execute CPU-bound functions at all
Each process has its own Python interpreter and GIL, so processes can run on separate cores
Threads are limited to a single CPU core by the operating system
questions.explanation: Each process gets its own interpreter and GIL, so multiple processes can truly run in parallel across CPU cores, unlike threads which share one GIL.

questions.question: Given `await asyncio.gather(task("A", 1), task("B", 1), task("C", 1))` where each task awaits a 1-second sleep, about how long does `main()` take?
options: ~0 seconds, because gather skips the sleeps
~3 seconds, because gather runs tasks one at a time
~2 seconds, because only two tasks overlap
~1 second, because the tasks run concurrently
questions.explanation: asyncio.gather runs the coroutines concurrently on the event loop, so with 1s sleeps each, the total is about 1s, not 3s.

questions.question: Which built-in module is best suited for precisely timing how long a small code snippet takes to run?
questions.explanation: timeit runs a snippet many times and reports the average, avoiding the noise of a single time.time() measurement.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the `else` clause attached to a `for` loop in Python?

It runs after every iteration of the loop

It runs only if the loop body raises an exception

questions.question: In `for n in range(2, 20): if n % 7 == 0: print(f"first multiple of 7: {n}"); break` (with an else printing 'no multiple of 7 found'), what gets printed?

questions.explanation: break exits the loop early, which causes the attached else block to be skipped entirely.

lessons.title: Python's `==` and `is` are NOT the same thing
lessons.description:

questions.question: Why does `5 is 5.0` evaluate to False even though `5 == 5.0` evaluates to True?
options: `is` only works on strings, not numbers
`5.0` is not a valid Python value
`is` and `==` are just different syntax for the same comparison
`is` compares object identity/type, while `==` compares value equality
questions.explanation: == checks whether two values are equal, while is checks whether they are the exact same object of the same type — an int and a float are never the same object.

questions.question:
What do these two lines print?
print(5 == 5.0)
print(5 is 5.0)
questions.explanation: 5 == 5.0 is True because the values are equal, but 5 is 5.0 is False because an int and a float are different objects/types.

questions.question: Which operator checks whether two names refer to the exact same object, rather than comparing values?

options: The order Python searches scopes when resolving a name: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in
The four types of Python data structures
The order functions are called in a recursive program
The order exceptions are checked in a try block
questions.explanation: LEGB stands for Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in — the sequence Python searches through to resolve a variable name.

Python raises an error because the file already exists
New content is appended to the end of the file

lessons.title: Python try/except Has 2 Hidden Keywords
lessons.description:
Most people stop at try and except in Python -- but else and finally unlock cleaner error handling. else runs only when nothing goes wrong, keeping success logic out of your risky code, while finally guarantees cleanup runs every single time. Watch the full breakdown and grab the runnable code in the source lesson below.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/python-mastery-path/level-1/08-error-handling/

#Shorts

questions.question: In a try/except/else/finally block, when does the `else` clause run?
options: Only if the finally block also runs
Only if an exception is caught
Only if the try block completes without raising an exception
Every time, regardless of whether an exception occurred
questions.explanation: The else clause executes only when the try block succeeds with no exception raised.

options: conversion failed, then this always runs
conversion succeeded: 42, then this always runs
this always runs, then conversion succeeded: 42
questions.explanation: Since int("42") doesn't raise, the else block runs first printing the success message, then finally always runs afterward.

questions.question: Which built-in exception does `int("abc")` raise?
questions.explanation: ValueError is raised when a value has the right type but an inappropriate value, such as a non-numeric string passed to int().

lessons.title: Why Every Python Project Needs Its Own Virtual Env
lessons.description:
Installing Python packages globally feels fine, until two projects need different versions of the same library and everything breaks. This Short shows you how to create an isolated virtual environment, install packages inside it, and freeze the exact versions with pip so anyone can rebuild your setup perfectly. It's one habit that saves hours of "works on my machine" debugging.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/python-mastery-path/level-1/09-modules-packages/

#Shorts

questions.question: Why should every Python project use its own virtual environment?
options: To make the project's code run faster
So each project's dependencies stay isolated and don't clash with other projects
Because pip requires a virtual environment to install any package
Because Python cannot run without a virtual environment
questions.explanation: A virtual environment isolates a project's installed packages, preventing version conflicts between different projects' dependencies.

questions.question: What does running `pip freeze > requirements.txt` accomplish?
options: It deletes unused packages from the virtual environment
It saves the exact versions of installed dependencies so the environment can be recreated elsewhere
It upgrades all installed packages to their latest versions
It installs every package listed in requirements.txt
questions.explanation: pip freeze lists installed packages with their exact versions, and redirecting it to requirements.txt lets you later run pip install -r requirements.txt to recreate the same environment.

questions.question: Which file marks a folder as a Python package so it can be imported with dotted notation?
questions.explanation: __init__.py marks a directory as a package, even when left empty, enabling imports like `from myapp import shapes`.

lessons.title: Build a Python To-Do App That Actually Remembers Tasks
lessons.description:
Ever wonder how a command-line tool remembers your data between runs? This Short breaks down the persistence pattern behind a simple Python to-do app -- one function to load JSON, one to save it, and a safe way to delete items without ever crashing on a bad task number. It's the CLI To-Do App project from Level 1 of the Python Mastery Path.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/python-mastery-path/level-1/10-project-todo-app/

#Shorts

questions.question: Why does load_tasks() catch json.JSONDecodeError and return an empty list instead?
options: So a corrupted or empty tasks.json file doesn't crash the app on startup
Because JSON files can't store lists of dictionaries
Because save_tasks() always leaves the file in an invalid state
Because Python requires every exception to be caught before printing
questions.explanation: Catching the decode error lets the app fall back to an empty task list instead of crashing on a bad file.

questions.question: In delete_task, what happens if you call delete_task(tasks, 99) but there are only 2 tasks?
options: It prints "No task with number 99" because the IndexError is caught
It silently deletes the last task instead
It adds a new empty task at position 99
It raises an unhandled IndexError and crashes the program
questions.explanation: delete_task wraps tasks.pop(index - 1) in a try/except IndexError, printing a friendly message instead of crashing.

questions.question: Which standard library module does storage.py use to persist tasks between runs?
questions.explanation: storage.py uses json.loads/json.dumps to read and write tasks.json.

lessons.title: Python Classes Can Use +, ==, and print() Too
lessons.description:
Ever wonder how Python's built-in types support +, ==, and print() so naturally? You can give your own classes the exact same powers with a handful of dunder methods. This Short walks through a Vector class that adds, compares, and prints itself using nothing but plain Python.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/python-mastery-path/level-2/01-oop/

#Shorts

questions.question: What is the purpose of dunder methods like __add__ and __eq__ on a class?
options: They are required for every Python class to be instantiated
They convert instance attributes into class attributes
They let custom objects integrate with Python's built-in syntax such as + and ==
They speed up attribute access through caching
questions.explanation: Dunder methods hook your objects into built-in operators and functions like +, ==, len(), and print().

questions.question: Given v1 = Vector(1, 2) and v2 = Vector(3, 4), what does print(v1 + v2) output?
questions.explanation: __add__ returns a new Vector(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y), and __repr__ formats it as Vector(4, 6).

questions.question: Which dunder method is triggered when you call len(obj) on an instance?
questions.explanation: __len__ defines what len() returns for a custom object, like Vector returning int((x**2+y**2)**0.5).

lessons.title: Why This Python Line Builds Nothing (On Purpose)
lessons.description:
List comprehensions build everything right away -- generator expressions don't. This Short shows the exact code where swapping brackets for parentheses turns instant computation into pure laziness, one value at a time. Perfect if you've ever wondered why some Python one-liners feel instant and others feel invisible.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/python-mastery-path/level-2/02-comprehensions-generators/

#Shorts

lessons.title: How Python decorators secretly work (in one line)
lessons.description:
That `@` symbol above a function isn't magic — it's just one function wrapping another, made possible because Python treats functions as regular objects. In under a minute we time a function's execution without touching a single line inside it, then reveal the plain Python underneath the decorator syntax. Full section on functional programming — closures, map/filter, and decorators — linked below.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/python-mastery-path/level-2/03-functional-programming/

#Shorts

lessons.title: Python's @contextmanager: Cleanup That Always Runs
lessons.description:
You already use `with` to auto-close files -- but you can build the exact same guaranteed-cleanup behavior yourself with one decorator and a single `yield`. No class, no `__enter__`/`__exit__` boilerplate, and the cleanup still fires even if the code inside raises an exception. This is straight from the Custom Exceptions & Context Managers lesson in Python Mastery Path Level 2.

lessons.description:
Python's built-in json module turns a dictionary into a JSON string and back again with just one function call each way. In this Short we run json.dumps and json.loads on a real example and see the round trip come back exactly as it started. The full lesson also covers CSV and XML if you want to go deeper.

lessons.title: Why re.match() silently returns None (regex trap)
lessons.description:
re.match() only checks the very start of a string -- if your pattern isn't literally at position zero, it fails silently and returns None, even when the text is right there. re.search() is almost always what you actually want. This is one of the most common regex bugs in Python, and it's an easy fix once you see it.

questions.question: Why is a plain Python module often the simplest way to implement a Singleton?
options: Because a module is only ever imported once and cached in sys.modules
Because modules automatically call __new__ exactly one time
Because classes cannot share state across instances
Because Python modules compile to a single bytecode object
questions.explanation: A module is cached the first time it's imported, so every import sees the same shared state without needing a class at all.

questions.question: In the SQL injection example, what happens if an attacker submits username = "' OR '1'='1" into an f-string query?
options: The database raises a syntax error and blocks the query
The query returns every row in the users table
The ORM automatically escapes the input and blocks the injection
Only the attacker's own row is returned
questions.explanation: Building SQL with an f-string lets the injected condition '1'='1' make the WHERE clause always true, returning every row.

questions.question: Which pytest fixture scope creates the fixture once per test file, shared across all tests in it?
questions.explanation: A module-scoped fixture is created once per test file, useful for expensive setup that multiple tests in that file can safely share.

lessons.title: Write More Pythonic Code: Comprehensions, Functional Tools & Clean Error Handling
lessons.description:
A guided tour through three habits that separate code that merely works from code that reads like Python: comprehensions and generators instead of manual loops, functional tools like map, filter, and reduce, and exception handling that actually tells you what went wrong. questions.question: Why does a generator expression use less memory than the equivalent list comprehension?
options: It produces values lazily, one at a time, instead of building the full sequence upfront
Python automatically compiles generator expressions to C code
It stores values as bytes instead of integers
It deletes each value from memory right after printing it
questions.explanation: A generator expression builds nothing until values are requested, unlike a list comprehension which builds the entire list immediately.

questions.question: What value does reduce(lambda acc, n: acc * n, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 1) produce?
questions.explanation: reduce multiplies the numbers together starting from the explicit start value 1, giving 1*1*2*3*4*5 = 120.

questions.explanation: Any object with __enter__ and __exit__ can act as a context manager, and __exit__ can also decide whether to suppress an exception.

lessons.title: That weird `if __name__ == "__main__"` line, explained
lessons.description:
Every Python script seems to end with this strange line. Here's what it actually does and why it matters the moment your file gets imported somewhere else.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/python-mastery-path/level-1/01-setup/

#Shorts

questions.question: Why do Python scripts commonly use the `if __name__ == "__main__":` guard?
options: So the interpreter can detect syntax errors before running
So the code inside only runs when the file is executed directly, not when it's imported
So function definitions are hidden from other files
questions.explanation: The guard lets a file be safely imported as a module elsewhere without automatically running its top-level script logic.

questions.question: Given hello.py defines greet() and calls print(greet("world")) inside the __main__ guard, what does `python3 hello.py` print?
options: Nothing, because greet is never called
questions.explanation: Running the file directly sets __name__ to "__main__", so the guarded print(greet("world")) executes and outputs Hello, world!.

questions.question: Which special variable does Python set to "__main__" only when a file is run directly?
questions.explanation: Python sets __name__ to "__main__" for the directly executed file, and to the module's name when it's imported instead.

lessons.title: The #1 Python string bug beginners hit
lessons.description:
Calling s.upper() doesn't change s. Strings in Python are immutable -- every string method returns a brand new string, and if you don't reassign it, nothing happens.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/python-mastery-path/level-1/06-strings-formatting/

#Shorts

questions.question: Why must you write s = s.upper() instead of just s.upper() to keep the change?
options: Because Python discards return values from string methods otherwise
Because strings are immutable, so methods return a new string rather than modifying the original
Because upper() is a static method that requires assignment
questions.explanation: Strings can't be modified in place, so every string method returns a brand-new string that must be reassigned to keep it.

questions.question: After running s = "hello" then s.upper() without reassigning, what is the value of s?
questions.explanation: s.upper() returns a new string but doesn't change s in place, so s still holds the original "hello".

questions.question: Which string method removes leading and trailing whitespace, returning a new string?
questions.explanation: strip() returns a new string with leading and trailing whitespace removed, leaving the original string untouched.

lessons.title: The Python data structure trick most tutorials skip
lessons.description:
Tuples aren't just "immutable lists" -- being immutable makes them hashable, which means they can be dictionary keys and set members. Lists never can.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/python-mastery-path/level-1/05-data-structures/

#Shorts

questions.question: Why can tuples be used as dictionary keys while lists cannot?
options: Tuples store only numbers, which are always hashable
Dictionaries only accept keys that support indexing
Tuples are immutable and therefore hashable, while lists are mutable and unhashable
Lists are too large to hash efficiently
questions.explanation: Tuples are hashable when their contents are, which is what makes them usable as dict keys or set members, unlike mutable lists.

questions.question: What does `locations = {(0, 0): "origin", (1, 1): "corner"}` demonstrate about tuples?
options: Tuples must be converted to strings before use as keys
Tuples can be used directly as dictionary keys
Dictionaries can only have tuple keys, never strings
Tuples automatically unpack into separate keys
questions.explanation: Because tuples are hashable, they can be used directly as dictionary keys, as shown by the (0, 0) and (1, 1) keys.

questions.question: Per the 'choosing the right structure' guidance, which type should you use for ordered data that allows duplicates and will change?
questions.explanation: A list is ordered, allows duplicates, and is mutable, making it the right choice when the data needs to change.

lessons.description:
Rust doesn't have a garbage collector -- so how does it stop memory bugs before they happen? By enforcing one rule at compile time: every value has exactly one owner. Watch what happens when you assign a String to a second variable, and how `.clone()` gives you an explicit way around it. lessons.title: Rust's loop can literally return a value

In most languages a loop just... loops. In Rust, `loop` can hand you back a value the moment you `break` with one -- no temp variable, no flag, just a straight assignment. This is one of the small ideas that makes Rust's "everything is an expression" philosophy click.

lessons.title: The Sneaky Semicolon That Breaks Rust Functions
lessons.description:
In Rust, the last expression in a function body is automatically returned -- no `return` keyword needed, as long as you leave off the semicolon. Add that semicolon back in and the exact same code silently returns nothing instead of the value you expected. This Short breaks down the statement-vs-expression rule that trips up almost every new Rust developer.

lessons.title: Rust's entry().or_insert() Is Basically Magic

Counting things in a HashMap in Rust doesn't need an if-key-exists check. lessons.title: SQLite Looks Broken Until You Run These 2 Lines
lessons.description:
SQLite's default output looks like a misaligned mess until you flip two settings. In this lesson we set up sqlite3, create a table, and prove your data survives even after you quit the shell -- because a SQLite database is just a file.

Source lesson(s):
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/sql-mastery-path/level-1/01-setup-first-queries/

#Shorts

questions.question: Why doesn't running `sqlite3 school.db` on a brand-new filename create the file right away?
options: The file is created only after you run .quit
SQLite only writes the file to disk the moment you write data to it
You must explicitly run CREATE DATABASE before opening it
SQLite requires you to run .tables first
questions.explanation: Opening the file alone doesn't touch the disk — SQLite creates it the moment data is actually written.

questions.question: What do `.mode column` and `.headers on` do when run inside the sqlite3 shell?
options: They pretty-print query results in aligned columns with column names shown above them
They create a new table to store query history
They turn on logging of every SQL statement to a file
questions.explanation: Column mode aligns the output and headers-on labels each column, making results far easier to read than the raw default.

questions.question: In the sqlite3 shell, what actually marks the end of a SQL statement?
questions.explanation: SQL statements can span multiple lines; it's the semicolon, not the newline, that ends them.

lessons.title: SQLite Lets You Put Text in an INTEGER Column (Seriously)
lessons.description:
SQLite doesn't enforce column types the way Postgres or MySQL do -- it uses "type affinity" instead, which means a column declared INTEGER will happily store text if you insert it. We create a table with five different declared types, insert mismatched values, and use typeof() to see exactly what SQLite actually stored. Useful to know before you assume your schema is protecting you.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/sql-mastery-path/level-1/02-select-basics-data-types/

#Shorts

questions.question: Why is listing exact column names preferred over `SELECT *` in real application code?
options: It's explicit about what's needed and won't silently change behavior if a column is added later
It always executes faster than SELECT *
It enforces strict data types on the columns
questions.explanation: Naming columns explicitly protects application code from unexpectedly picking up new columns added to the table later.

questions.question: What would `SELECT title || ' by ' || author AS citation FROM books;` return for the row with title 'Dune' and author 'Frank Herbert'?
questions.explanation: The `||` operator concatenates strings, so the literal text ' by ' is inserted between title and author.

questions.question: Which keyword explicitly converts a value to a different type, as in `CAST('42' AS INTEGER)`?
questions.explanation: CAST is the portable, explicit way to convert types rather than relying on SQLite's implicit type coercion.

lessons.title: The SQL NULL Bug That Breaks WHERE Clauses
lessons.description:
Ever run a WHERE genre = NULL query that always returns zero rows, even though the data is right there? This is one of the most common silent bugs in SQL, and it's caused by how NULL actually works. In this Short we break down why equals can't compare to NULL, and the two operators -- IS NULL and IS NOT NULL -- that actually work.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/sql-mastery-path/level-1/03-filtering-where/

#Shorts

questions.question: Why does `WHERE genre = NULL` fail to match rows even when a genre column is actually NULL?
options: The comparison causes a SQL syntax error
NULL represents 'unknown,' so nothing can be known to equal an unknown value
= NULL only works in Postgres, not SQLite
NULL is stored internally as the empty string
questions.explanation: You must use IS NULL because equality comparisons against an unknown value never evaluate to true.

questions.question: What does `WHERE author LIKE '_ea%'` match?
options: Authors whose 2nd character is 'e' and 3rd character is 'a'
questions.explanation: The underscore matches exactly one character, so '_ea%' requires any first letter, then 'e', then 'a', then anything.

questions.question: Which clause tests whether a value falls inclusively within a range, equivalent to combining >= and <= with AND?
questions.explanation: BETWEEN x AND y includes both endpoints, matching the same rows as `>= x AND <= y`.

lessons.title: The SQL Mistake That Makes LIMIT Useless
lessons.description:
LIMIT looks simple, but on its own it doesn't promise you anything -- the database can hand back any rows it feels like. Here's the one keyword you need to pair it with to get the same, predictable top rows every single time.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/sql-mastery-path/level-1/04-sorting-limiting/

#Shorts

questions.question: Why should LIMIT almost always be paired with an ORDER BY clause?
options: LIMIT only works on tables that are already sorted on disk
Without ORDER BY, the specific rows LIMIT returns are arbitrary
ORDER BY must be written before LIMIT is legal SQL
LIMIT throws an error if ORDER BY is missing
questions.explanation: LIMIT just caps the row count from whatever order the rows arrive in, so without ORDER BY there's no guarantee which rows you get.

questions.question: What does `SELECT title, price FROM books ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3;` return?
options: Rows 3 through 6 in alphabetical order by title
It skips the 3 highest-priced books, then returns the next 3
questions.explanation: OFFSET 3 skips the first 3 rows of the descending price order before LIMIT 3 takes the next batch.

questions.question: In the fixed clause order of a query, which clause must appear immediately before ORDER BY?
questions.explanation: The query is written as SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT ..., so WHERE precedes ORDER BY.

lessons.title: SQL's WHERE Can't Filter COUNT(*) -- Here's the Fix
lessons.description:
Ever written WHERE COUNT(*) greater than 2 to filter grouped results and watched SQL reject it outright? It's not a typo problem -- it's about when aggregates actually exist during query evaluation. This clip covers the one-word fix from Level 1 of the SQL Mastery Path's aggregates and GROUP BY lesson.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/sql-mastery-path/level-1/05-aggregates-group-by/

#Shorts

questions.question: Why is `SELECT genre, COUNT(*) FROM books WHERE COUNT(*) > 2 GROUP BY genre;` invalid?
options: GROUP BY must come before WHERE in the statement
Aggregate results like COUNT(*) don't exist yet at the point WHERE is evaluated
COUNT(*) is not a real SQL function
questions.explanation: WHERE filters rows before grouping happens, so it can't see aggregate values that are only computed afterward — that's what HAVING is for.

questions.question: If some rows in `books` have a NULL genre, what's the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(genre) in `SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_rows, COUNT(genre) AS rows_with_genre FROM books;`?
options: They always return the same number
COUNT(genre) counts only distinct genre values
COUNT(*) counts every row including NULL genres, while COUNT(genre) skips rows where genre is NULL
COUNT(*) throws an error when any column contains NULL
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows regardless of NULLs, but COUNT(column) only counts rows where that column is not NULL.

questions.question: Which clause filters groups after aggregation, rather than filtering individual rows beforehand?
questions.explanation: HAVING runs after GROUP BY has produced aggregate values, letting you filter on things like COUNT(*) or AVG(price).

lessons.title: SQL Fundamentals in 9 Minutes: Queries to GROUP BY
lessons.description:
New to SQL? This walkthrough takes you from a blank terminal to writing real, useful queries -- entirely with the free sqlite3 command-line tool, no server or account required. We install SQLite and create a first table, then learn how SELECT actually works (aliases, computed columns, DISTINCT, type casting), how to filter rows precisely with WHERE (comparisons, AND/OR/NOT, BETWEEN, IN, LIKE, NULL checks), how to control result order and size with ORDER BY, LIMIT, and OFFSET, and finally how to summarize data with COUNT, SUM, AVG, GROUP BY, and HAVING. Every query shown is copy-paste runnable against the same small books table, and each section builds directly on the last -- by the end you'll be able to design, filter, sort, and summarize your own tables using nothing but the command line.

Lessons covered in this video:

- 02 - SELECT Basics & Data Types: https://sigilipelli.github.io/sql-mastery-path/level-1/02-select-basics-data-types/
- 03 - Filtering with WHERE: https://sigilipelli.github.io/sql-mastery-path/level-1/03-filtering-where/
- 04 - Sorting & Limiting Results: https://sigilipelli.github.io/sql-mastery-path/level-1/04-sorting-limiting/
- 05 - Aggregate Functions & GROUP BY: https://sigilipelli.github.io/sql-mastery-path/level-1/05-aggregates-group-by/

questions.question: Because a SQLite database is just a plain file, what happens to your data after you `.quit` and then reopen that same file?
options: You must re-run every CREATE TABLE statement again
The data is lost unless you explicitly saved it first
Only the table schema persists, not the rows
All the data persists and is still there
questions.explanation: Closing the shell doesn't erase the file — reopening it shows everything you previously created and inserted.

questions.question: A `demo` table has column `e` declared as NUMERIC but a string `'still works'` is inserted into it. What does `SELECT typeof(e) FROM demo;` report?
questions.explanation: SQLite uses flexible type affinity rather than strict column types, so it stores and reports the string as text even though the column is NUMERIC.

questions.question: Which clause splits rows into buckets so that aggregate functions like COUNT() or AVG() are computed separately for each bucket?
questions.explanation: GROUP BY buckets rows by column value, and each aggregate function then runs once per bucket instead of once for the whole table.

lessons.title: Why Bash Says 'Command Not Found' For Your Own Script
lessons.description:
You wrote the script, saved it, and bash still refuses to run it -- even though the file is sitting right there. Turns out every shell script needs two tiny things: a shebang line and the executable bit, plus the dot-slash to tell bash "run the one right here." This is the exact first-script walkthrough from Level 1 of the Shell Mastery Path.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/shell-mastery-path/level-1/01-setup/

#Shorts

questions.question: Why does plain `hello.sh` (without `./`) fail to run even after `chmod +x hello.sh`?
options: The current directory isn't normally on your PATH
The file is missing a shebang line
Only root can execute any script
chmod +x only applies to directories, not files
questions.explanation: Bash only looks for bare commands on PATH, and the current directory isn't on it by default, so you need `./hello.sh` to point at it explicitly.

questions.question: Given `chmod +x hello.sh` then `ls -l hello.sh` shows `-rwxr-xr-x`, what do the three 'x' characters mean?
options: The file has been run exactly three times
The file is executable only by root
The file is hidden from normal listings
Owner, group, and other can all execute the file
questions.explanation: Each 'x' in the permission string grants execute access to owner, group, and other respectively.

questions.question: What is the special first line `#!/usr/bin/env bash` in a script called?
questions.explanation: This line is called the shebang, and it tells the OS which interpreter to use when the script is run directly.

lessons.title: Bash Quotes Aren't Interchangeable (This Will Bite You)
lessons.description:
In bash, single quotes and double quotes are NOT the same thing -- one expands variables, the other treats everything as literal text. Mix them up and your script can print the wrong value with zero errors to warn you. This is one of the first habits every shell scripter needs to lock in.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/shell-mastery-path/level-1/02-variables-data-types/

#Shorts

questions.question: Why does writing `name = "Ada"` (with spaces around `=`) cause a syntax error in Bash?
options: Bash parses it as running a command named `name` with arguments `=` and `Ada"`
Spaces are reserved for defining arrays
Bash requires all variable names to be uppercase
questions.explanation: Bash treats the spaces as argument separators, so it tries to run `name` as a command instead of assigning a variable.

questions.question: For `food="fried rice"`, what is the risk of writing `echo $food` instead of `echo "$food"`?
options: Bash may word-split the value into multiple separate arguments
It throws a syntax error immediately
questions.explanation: Without quotes, Bash word-splits the value on spaces before passing it along, so "fried rice" can become two separate words.

questions.question: Inside `$(( a % b ))`, what does the `%` operator compute?
options: A percentage of a relative to b
The remainder of a divided by b
a raised to the power of b
The average of a and b
questions.explanation: In Bash arithmetic expansion, `%` is the modulo operator, returning the remainder of integer division.

lessons.title: Bash Trick: Skip `if` With && and ||
lessons.description:
Every command in bash already returns a hidden exit status -- and you can react to it directly with && and ||, no if statement required. This Short walks through the exact one-liner pattern from the Shell Mastery Path's control flow lesson, using a real grep-based example. Perfect if you're tired of writing three-line if blocks for a single check.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/shell-mastery-path/level-1/03-control-flow/

#Shorts

questions.question: Why is `[[ ]]` generally preferred over `[ ]` in Bash scripts?
options: It avoids unquoted word-splitting issues and supports pattern/regex matching
It is required for numeric arithmetic comparisons
It is portable to plain POSIX `sh`, unlike `[ ]`
It always executes faster than any other test method
questions.explanation: `[[ ]]` is a bash extension that safely handles unquoted variables and adds pattern and regex matching that `[ ]` lacks.

questions.question:
What does this print?
count=5
if (( count % 2 == 0 )); then
    echo "even"
else
    echo "odd"
fi
questions.explanation: 5 % 2 equals 1, which is not 0, so the else branch runs and prints "odd".

questions.question: What symbol must terminate each branch inside a `case` statement in Bash?
questions.explanation: Each case branch ends with `;;`, while `esac` closes the entire case statement.

lessons.title: The Bash Loop That Silently Breaks on Spaces
lessons.description:
You've written this bash for-loop a hundred times: for x in $(command); do ... done. It works great in every demo -- until a filename or a line of output has a space in it. See the word-splitting trap and the while-read fix that actually holds up on real data.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/shell-mastery-path/level-1/04-loops/

#Shorts

questions.question: Why does the idiomatic file-reading pattern `while IFS= read -r line; do ... done < file` set `IFS=`?
options: To split each line on commas automatically
To enable regular expression matching on the line
To prevent leading and trailing whitespace from being stripped from each line
To make the loop execute noticeably faster
questions.explanation: Setting IFS to empty stops Bash from trimming whitespace, so each line is read exactly as it appears in the file.

questions.question:
What does this loop print?
for i in {1..10}; do
    if (( i == 5 )); then
        break
    fi
    echo "$i"
done
questions.explanation: The loop breaks entirely as soon as i reaches 5, so only 1 through 4 get printed.

questions.question: Which keyword skips the rest of the current loop iteration and moves on to the next one?
questions.explanation: `continue` skips whatever code remains in the current iteration and jumps straight to the next one.

lessons.title: $@ vs $*: One Character That Breaks Your Bash Script
lessons.description:
Quoting your Bash function arguments wrong can silently mangle multi-word arguments without throwing a single error. This Short breaks down the difference between the quoted all-arguments variable and the star variable, and why only one of them is safe to use when forwarding arguments in your scripts.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/shell-mastery-path/level-1/05-functions-arguments/

#Shorts

questions.question: Why should you use `local` for variables assigned inside a Bash function?
options: It is required syntax for every variable in a function
Without it, variables assigned inside a function are global by default, risking bugs
It makes the function execute faster
It automatically makes the variable readonly
questions.explanation: Bash function variables leak into the global scope unless declared with `local`, which can silently overwrite outer variables.

questions.question:
What does the final line print?
counter=0
bump() {
    local counter=100
    ((counter++))
    echo "inside: $counter"
}
bump
echo "outside: $counter"
questions.explanation: The `local counter=100` inside bump() shadows the outer counter, so the global counter stays untouched at 0.

questions.question: Which form correctly forwards all positional arguments while preserving arguments that contain spaces as separate words?
questions.explanation: Quoted "$@" expands each positional parameter as its own separately-quoted word, unlike "$*" which joins them into one string.

questions.question: What must be true about the shebang line for it to correctly tell the OS which interpreter to use?
options: It must be the very first line of the file, with no blank line before it
It must appear right before the `main` function
It must be written as a regular comment anywhere in the script
questions.explanation: The shebang only works if it's the literal first line of the file; any blank line before it breaks the mechanism.

questions.question:
What happens when you run this?
readonly PI=3.14159
PI=3
options: Bash prints an error: PI: readonly variable
PI silently stays 3.14159 with no error
questions.explanation: Once a variable is declared readonly, any later attempt to reassign it produces an error instead of changing its value.

questions.question: Why can't `return` be used to hand back a computed string value from a Bash function?
options: return always resets the value to 0 regardless of what's given
return only sets a numeric exit status (0-255), not arbitrary data
return is not supported inside functions at all
return can only be used in the top-level script, never in a function
questions.explanation: To hand back an actual value like a string or number, you print it with echo/printf and capture it with command substitution instead of return.

lessons.title: TypeScript Catches Bugs Before Your Code Even Runs
lessons.description:
TypeScript type-checks your code, then erases every type it used to do it -- the JavaScript that ships has none of it left. Watch a one-line mistake get caught by the compiler before it ever reaches production, straight from the first lesson of the TypeScript Mastery Path.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/typescript-mastery-path/level-1/01-setup/

#Shorts

lessons.title: This TypeScript Compiles Fine. Then It Crashes at Runtime.
lessons.description:
TypeScript's `any` type looks harmless -- until it lets you call a number like a function and the compiler says nothing. We break down why `any` is a hole in your safety net, and why `unknown` is the type-safe fix that forces you to check before you touch.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/typescript-mastery-path/level-1/02-basic-types/

#Shorts

lessons.title: TypeScript Reads Your Mind Inside an if Statement
lessons.description:
Ever notice how TypeScript just knows what type a variable is inside an if block, with zero casts? That's control flow analysis narrowing a string-or-number union down to exactly one type per branch. Watch it happen with a real formatId function, then go try it yourself.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/typescript-mastery-path/level-1/03-control-flow/

#Shorts

lessons.title: One Function, Two Totally Different Call Signatures
lessons.description:
TypeScript lets a single function accept completely different argument shapes -- and still stops you cold if you mix them up. This Short breaks down function overloads using a makeDate() example: one signature for a timestamp, another for year/month/day, and one implementation underneath that handles both safely.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/typescript-mastery-path/level-1/04-functions-type-annotations/

#Shorts

lessons.title: TypeScript Checks Shape, Not Name (Structural Typing)
lessons.description:
TypeScript doesn't care whether you explicitly declared an object as a certain interface -- it only cares whether the object has the right shape. This is structural typing, one of the most distinctive (and surprising) parts of TypeScript's type system compared to nominal languages like Java or C#. See the full breakdown, plus optional properties, readonly fields, and interface extension, in the source lesson below.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/typescript-mastery-path/level-1/05-interfaces-type-aliases/
